title: SnowflakeClear
question: How does a snowflake get its shape?
hook: Every snowflake is a tiny recording of the weather it fell through. Watch six arms grow the same way, because they all feel the same air.

explainer.title: It starts with water
explainer.text: A water molecule is bent, with about 104.5 degrees between its hydrogens. Hydrogen bonds link each molecule to four neighbours, and that frame is built from six-sided rings. So ice crystals are hexagonal.

explainer.title: A speck grows
explainer.text: A crystal starts as a tiny hexagon on a speck of dust. Corners poke into fresher, moister air, catch more vapour and race ahead. That runaway makes branches. The model runs this rule on a hexagonal grid.

explainer.title: Temperature picks the shape
explainer.text: In the 1930s Ukichiro Nakaya grew snow in a cold lab and found shapes flip with temperature and humidity. Roughly: plates near minus 2, needles near minus 5, columns after that, plates and ferns near minus 15.

explainer.title: Six arms, one journey
explainer.text: The arms do not signal each other. The flake is small and travels as one piece, so all six arms meet the same air at the same moment and grow the same way. The shape records its path.

explainer.title: No two alike?
explainer.text: Wilson Bentley found no two flakes the same after photographing thousands from 1885. But alike is not identical, and twins can grow side by side. Nancy Knight's 1988 paper was about near-matches, not exact ones.

explainer.title: Clear ice, white snow
explainer.text: Many snowflakes are broken, rimed or clumped, not neat stars. And snow looks white because countless faces scatter every colour of light, even though each crystal is clear.

concepts.def: A weak pull between a hydrogen on one water molecule and the oxygen of another.
The ordinary form of ice, whose oxygen atoms sit in a hexagonal lattice.
A pattern that looks the same after turning by 60 degrees.
Air holding more water vapour than it could in balance with ice, which drives crystals to grow.
A bump on a growing crystal reaches fresher vapour, grows faster and sticks out more, so edges break into branches.
A grid of cells that each follow the same simple rule using only their neighbours.
The overall shape type of a crystal, such as plate, column or needle.
A map of crystal shape against temperature and humidity, named for Ukichiro Nakaya.
A branching, fern-like pattern, from the Greek word for tree.
Ice formed when supercooled cloud droplets freeze onto a crystal.
